Family Health

Melanoma: understanding skin changes, stages and treatment

Updated: October 7, 2026

Written and edited by BeMama Authors team: checked against published guidance from recognized health organizations.

Melanoma begins in pigment-producing cells called melanocytes. Most melanomas arise in the skin, although rarer forms occur in the eye or mucosal tissues. This article focuses on skin melanoma. Early recognition is valuable, but you cannot reliably decide whether a spot is harmless or determine a cancer stage by looking at it yourself.

Look beyond a dark mole

Melanoma can appear as a changing mole or a new spot, and not every melanoma is darkly pigmented. A lesion that grows, changes, itches, bleeds or looks unlike your other marks deserves assessment. Changes on the palms, soles or around nails should also be taken seriously.

The ABCDE reminder refers to asymmetry, irregular borders, varied color, diameter and evolution. A diameter larger than about 6 mm can be a warning sign, but smaller melanomas occur. Do not wait for a spot to meet every feature before booking an examination.

Understand what establishes the diagnosis

A clinician examines the skin, often with a dermatoscope, and may recommend removing a suspicious lesion for laboratory examination. Pathology identifies whether melanoma is present and reports features important for further care.

One key measurement is Breslow thickness: how deeply the tumor extends into the skin. Ulceration is another pathological feature, involving loss of the overlying surface. It is not simply a description of any scratch or bleeding caused by catching a mole on clothing.

Use stages as a guide to extent

Stage 0, or melanoma in situ, is confined to the outermost skin layer. Stages I and II describe invasive melanoma without identified regional or distant spread; thickness and ulceration help distinguish their subgroups. A single thickness cutoff cannot accurately summarize every subgroup.

Stage III involves regional spread, such as nearby lymph nodes or certain deposits in skin or lymphatic pathways. Stage IV involves distant spread. These categories apply to cutaneous melanoma; rare eye and mucosal melanomas have different assessment considerations.

TNM describes features of the primary tumour (T), regional lymph nodes (N) and distant metastasis (M). This is staging, which describes extent, rather than simply grading how abnormal cells look. Thickness and ulceration can move a tumour into different stage groups even when its width on the skin looks small.

Stage I includes relatively thin invasive tumours, while stage II includes thicker tumours or some thinner ones with ulceration, without established regional or distant spread. Statements such as “stage I is up to two millimetres” and “stage II is over one millimetre” overlap because ulceration and other details also matter. Ask for your actual stage and pathology explanation rather than assigning a stage from one measurement.

Distant spread can involve organs such as the lung or brain, or lymph nodes far from the original melanoma. Its outlook is more serious, but spread does not mean every person will have the same outcome or that modern treatment cannot help.

Ask why additional tests are recommended

A sentinel lymph-node biopsy may be discussed when the risk of microscopic spread justifies it. The procedure checks selected draining nodes and helps staging. It is not required for every melanoma, and a positive result does not automatically mean every nearby node must be removed.

Scans are also selected according to stage, symptoms and clinical circumstances. Ask what a proposed scan or procedure could change in the plan, as well as its risks. More testing is not always more useful for a low-risk early lesion.

PET, CT or MRI may be considered when their findings could change treatment; a PET scan detects patterns of tracer uptake rather than directly proving that every bright area is cancer. Sentinel-node assessment and imaging answer different questions.

Discuss treatment appropriate to the findings

Surgery removes the melanoma with a surrounding margin of normal-appearing skin. Some higher-risk early melanomas may also be considered for treatment to reduce recurrence. More advanced disease may need immunotherapy, targeted treatment when suitable tumor changes are present, or other selected approaches.

Radiotherapy, surgery and additional treatments have roles in particular circumstances. The choices depend on the extent, biology, previous treatment and overall health. Treatments have improved over time, so an old survival table should not be used as a personal forecast.

Surgery commonly treats stage 0 and early invasive disease, with node assessment and additional treatment selected for the findings. Some stage III disease can be removed surgically, and stage IV care may combine systemic treatment with procedures for particular sites. Conventional chemotherapy is used less often than modern immunotherapy or suitable targeted treatment; a clinical trial may also be discussed.

Five-year survival statistics describe groups followed after diagnosis and, when reported as relative survival, compare them with a similar general population. They do not mean someone has only five years to live. Older figures such as 99%, 65% and 25% for localised, regional and distant disease should not be presented as current individual predictions; stage, overall health, tumour biology, treatment advances and response all matter.

Continue skin protection and follow-up

Sun protection reduces ultraviolet damage: use shade, protective clothing and a suitable broad-spectrum sunscreen, and avoid tanning beds. These habits reduce risk but do not treat an existing melanoma or guarantee that it will not spread.

After treatment, follow the agreed skin and clinical examination schedule. Ask which changes to report and whether anyone should help check areas you cannot easily see. If a new or changing spot concerns you between appointments, contact the team rather than waiting solely for the next scheduled review.

Tell the team if your immune system is weakened, including by HIV or immune-suppressing medicines, because that may affect assessment and follow-up. Keep taking prescribed treatment unless your clinician changes the plan.

Evidence-informed guidance

What trusted health organizations recommend

NCI describes melanoma staging through tumour thickness, ulceration and regional or distant spread, with tests selected to guide care.

AAD warning signs support assessment of changing lesions, including small or non-dark lesions; sun protection cannot treat an existing melanoma.

How BeMama can help

Ask for the pathology report, an explanation of the stage and which tests or treatments could change your care.

When to seek help

Arrange prompt assessment of a new or changing suspicious lesion and report symptoms between planned follow-up visits.

Evidence notes updated: October 7, 2026

Key takeaways

  • Melanoma is not always a large dark mole.
  • Thickness, ulceration and spread contribute to staging.
  • Sun protection supports prevention; diagnosis and treatment require medical care.

Frequently asked questions

Can a spot smaller than 6 mm be melanoma?

Yes. Size is only one clue, and a new or changing lesion should be assessed.

Does sunscreen stop an existing melanoma from spreading?

No. It reduces UV exposure but cannot replace investigation or treatment of a suspicious lesion.

This article is general education, not medical advice, diagnosis, or treatment. Always talk with a qualified healthcare professional about your situation, and seek urgent care for emergencies.
